analyticsEmpty.nerd: No analytics:event payloads have been emitted yet.

text.nerd: The HUD is a reusable DOM overlay that reads from the shared GameState resource object.

text.kid: When something important happens, a fact card connects the game to the real world.
text.nerd: Fact cards are data-defined learning moments and emit analytics when opened.

imageAlt.kid: A bright mineral becoming a chip
imageAlt.nerd: Silicon source material represented as a chip precursor

summary.kid: The chip in a phone or computer begins with minerals pulled from the ground. Quartz can become the silicon wafer where tiny circuits are printed.
summary.nerd: Integrated circuits depend on ultra-pure silicon wafers, conductive metals, power materials, and process inputs that move through a long global supply chain.

deeper.kid: The cleaner the material gets, the better the chip can work.
deeper.nerd: Chip-grade silicon is refined far beyond ordinary industrial material because stray atoms can disrupt transistor behavior at nanometer scales.

subtitle.kid: Place miners, fill the basket, and learn what chips are made from.
subtitle.nerd: Allocate limited extraction capacity across mineral deposits while managing budget and energy.

noDeposit.kid: Click a gem cluster to inspect it.
noDeposit.nerd: Select a deposit to inspect mineral type, depth, remaining material, and placement cost.

insufficientResources.kid: Not enough credits for that miner yet.
insufficientResources.nerd: Placement rejected: operating budget is below miner cost.

alreadyMined.kid: That deposit already has a miner.
alreadyMined.nerd: Placement rejected: this deposit is already assigned.

depositNotFound.kid: That deposit could not be found.
depositNotFound.nerd: Placement rejected: deposit id is not present in chapter state.

text.kid: The clinic's Nova rack is dark, and the rescue starts underground. Get the materials moving.
text.nerd: Nova is offline. The recovery begins upstream, with mineral inputs that later become wafers, conductors, batteries, and specialty components.

text.kid: Fast is tempting, Sam. Four miner slots means every shortcut also creates a bottleneck.
text.nerd: Speed matters, but each extraction rig consumes capital and a slot. Deeper deposits can be richer, but they add energy load.

text.kid: Then I am filling the basket before the city loses another hour.
text.nerd: Then I am treating the basket as the production target. Resources carry into the refinery.

text.kid: And I will flag what is real and what is simplified, because a rescue still needs truth.
text.nerd: First extraction of each mineral unlocks a source-backed fact card, because urgency does not remove the need for honest abstractions.

imageAlt.kid: A white quartz gem turning into a silicon chip
imageAlt.nerd: Quartz represented as an upstream silicon input

summary.kid: Quartz is a common rock with silicon inside it. After many cleaning steps, silicon can become the wafer where circuits are printed.
summary.nerd: USGS describes silicon metal as a material that can be processed into ultra-high-purity polysilicon for semiconductor and solar grades.

deeper.kid: The chip is not carved from a rock. The rock starts a long cleaning and shaping journey.
deeper.nerd: The important lesson is transformation: mined silicon-bearing material must be refined into high-purity feedstock before crystal growth and wafer slicing.

imageAlt.kid: An orange copper gem with tiny wires
imageAlt.nerd: Copper represented as conductor feedstock

summary.kid: Copper is great at carrying electricity. Electronics use copper because signals need clear paths to move.
summary.nerd: USGS copper summaries track electrical and electronic products as a major copper end use, alongside construction and transportation.

deeper.kid: A chip needs tiny paths for electricity, and copper is one metal that helps make paths.
deeper.nerd: Copper's supply chain matters because conductors, interconnects, wiring, motors, and power systems all depend on reliable copper availability.

imageAlt.kid: A pink lithium gem beside a battery
imageAlt.nerd: Lithium represented as battery material

summary.kid: Lithium helps make rechargeable batteries. Chips need power, and many devices carry that power in batteries.
summary.nerd: USGS estimated that global lithium production rose sharply in 2025 in response to lithium-ion battery demand and added production capacity.

deeper.kid: Lithium is not the chip, but it helps phones, laptops, and electric cars use chips away from a wall plug.
deeper.nerd: Lithium shows why the semiconductor story is also an energy-storage story: mobile compute depends on both logic chips and battery chemistry.

imageAlt.kid: A blue cobalt gem on a world map
imageAlt.nerd: Cobalt represented with geographic supply concentration

summary.kid: Most mined cobalt comes from Congo. When one place supplies so much, companies have to watch the supply chain carefully.
summary.nerd: USGS 2026 data says Congo (Kinshasa) accounted for an estimated 73 percent of world mined cobalt output.

deeper.kid: A tiny chip can depend on choices made far away from the factory.
deeper.nerd: Cobalt teaches geographic concentration: material risk can come from production geography, refining geography, policy, labor issues, and logistics.

imageAlt.kid: A purple rare-earth gem with a magnet
imageAlt.nerd: Rare earths represented as magnet and specialty-material inputs

summary.kid: Rare earths help make strong magnets, screens, and special parts. They are not always rare, but they are hard to separate.
summary.nerd: USGS 2026 rare-earth summaries describe export controls and processing concerns, showing why separation capacity matters as much as mining.

deeper.kid: Finding the rock is only step one. Separating the useful pieces can be the hard part.
deeper.nerd: Rare earths are a supply-chain lesson in processing bottlenecks: ore, separation, oxides, metals, and magnets can each sit in different jurisdictions.

body.kid: You mined the first ingredients for a chip supply chain. Next, the refinery will clean and upgrade them.
body.nerd: Chapter 1 has produced the upstream mineral inventory. Chapter 2 converts raw input into higher-purity materials under energy and water constraints.

subtitle.kid: Build a clean path from rough minerals to pure material.
subtitle.nerd: Route raw inputs through staged processing while managing energy, water, and waste.

laneNotFound.nerd: Placement rejected: refinery lane id was not found.

columnOutOfBounds.kid: That spot is outside the grid.
columnOutOfBounds.nerd: Placement rejected: column is outside the configured grid.

cellOccupied.kid: That spot already has a machine.
cellOccupied.nerd: Placement rejected: selected cell is already occupied.

inactiveSequence.kid: Start from the left. This machine will not run yet.
inactiveSequence.nerd: Placement rejected: modules only activate in a connected left-to-right chain.

insufficientResources.kid: Not enough credits for that machine.
insufficientResources.nerd: Placement rejected: budget is below module cost.

insufficientEnergyWater.kid: The line needs more energy or water.
insufficientEnergyWater.nerd: Tick blocked: energy or water is below refinery demand.

insufficientMinerals.nerd: Tick blocked: the active lane lacks enough raw mineral input.

slagCapacity.kid: The slag pile is too full. Recycle or store some.
slagCapacity.nerd: Tick blocked: slag would exceed configured waste capacity.

text.kid: The rocks arrived. Can we just rush them into the chip line?
text.nerd: Mined feedstocks arrived. Can Nova recovery tolerate rough inputs, or do we lose reliability downstream?

text.kid: Only if you want bad chips. Place machines in order: speed has to answer to purity.
text.nerd: Build ordered processing chains. A lane runs only when the required modules are connected in sequence, so throughput has to answer to purity.

text.kid: Fine, but every clean step burns power and water the city also needs.
text.nerd: Purification is constrained by utility inputs and waste handling. The rescue consumes the same infrastructure it is trying to support.

text.kid: That is the tradeoff. Push toward nine nines, but watch the waste you create.
text.nerd: That is the tradeoff. The game target uses 9N purity shorthand, but the system cost is energy, water, and waste.

imageAlt.kid: A purity meter climbing toward nine nines
imageAlt.nerd: A 9N purity meter representing semiconductor-grade feedstock

summary.kid: Nine nines means the silicon is almost all silicon. Tiny wrong bits can mess up tiny chip parts.
summary.nerd: 9N is shorthand for 99.9999999 percent purity. Semiconductor manufacturing depends on highly controlled impurities, not random contamination.

deeper.kid: Clean material helps the next chapter grow a smooth crystal.
deeper.nerd: Purification prepares feedstock for crystal growth, where uncontrolled contaminants can affect electrical behavior and later wafer yield.

imageAlt.kid: A furnace connected to an energy meter
imageAlt.nerd: A refining line consuming electricity and water

summary.kid: Hot machines and chemical baths need power and water. If either runs low, the line slows down.
summary.nerd: Refining economics are shaped by energy prices, water access, reliability, and environmental compliance.

deeper.kid: This is why the place where refining happens matters.
deeper.nerd: Processing capacity often clusters where electricity, water, infrastructure, and permits make large-scale purification feasible.

title.nerd: Waste Handling and Recycling Reduce Loss

imageAlt.kid: A recycling arrow over a slag pile
imageAlt.nerd: Slag management represented as recycling and storage choices

summary.kid: The refinery leaves slag behind. Recycling can earn credits, but safe storage also matters.
summary.nerd: Processing waste can contain recoverable value, but unmanaged waste creates environmental and compliance risk.

deeper.kid: A clean supply chain is not only about making useful stuff. It is also about handling leftovers.
deeper.nerd: Recycling and storage decisions show the hidden material flows behind high-tech manufacturing.

body.kid: You cleaned the raw minerals and reached nine nines purity. Next, you will grow a crystal and slice wafers.
body.nerd: Chapter 2 produced purified feedstock and managed waste constraints. Chapter 3 turns that material into a crystal ingot and wafers.

subtitle.kid: Grow one clean silicon crystal, then slice it into wafers.
subtitle.nerd: Convert purified feedstock into a single-crystal ingot and wafer output for fabrication.

holdToPull.nerd: Hold pointer to pull seed crystal

releaseToCool.nerd: Release pointer to cool and stabilize

pullHint.kid: Hold to pull the seed. Release when the heat gets too high.
pullHint.nerd: Pull while temperature stays near the green band; release to cool and reduce defects.

sliceHint.kid: Tap the guide marks. Clean slices become wafers.
sliceHint.nerd: Select slice-guide centers. Flawed ingot sections are discarded.

flawedDiscard.kid: That slice hit a wobbly section, so it was discarded.
flawedDiscard.nerd: The selected ingot section was below the flaw threshold and produced no usable wafer.

missedGuide.kid: Too far from the guide line. Try the bright marks.
missedGuide.nerd: Slice attempt was outside guide tolerance.

alreadyCut.kid: That spot is already cut. Try a fresh guide mark.
alreadyCut.nerd: This slice guide was already used. Select an uncut segment.

insufficientEnergyWater.kid: The pull needs energy and cooling water.
insufficientEnergyWater.nerd: Crystal growth tick blocked by insufficient energy or water.

text.kid: The clean silicon is ready. If the crystal works, Nova gets a real foundation.
text.nerd: Purified feedstock is melted and recrystallized so Nova's wafer has a controlled atomic structure.

text.kid: Do not yank it. Hold steady: a fast pull can ruin what the refinery saved.
text.nerd: The Czochralski method pulls a seed crystal from molten silicon while thermal stability controls crystal quality.

text.kid: So I slow down now so the city can move faster later.
text.nerd: So the time spent controlling the ingot becomes fewer failures during later fabrication.

imageAlt.kid: A seed crystal being pulled from a glowing cup
imageAlt.nerd: Seed crystal pulled from molten silicon

summary.kid: A scientist named Jan Czochralski found a way to pull crystals from melted material.
summary.nerd: The Czochralski process grows a single crystal by drawing a seed from a melt under controlled temperature and rotation.

deeper.kid: One smooth crystal helps the next machines print tiny circuits.
deeper.nerd: Single-crystal silicon gives chipmakers a consistent lattice for later oxidation, lithography, etching, and doping steps.

title.nerd: Wafer Shape Comes From the Ingot

imageAlt.kid: Round wafer slices from a cylinder
imageAlt.nerd: Circular wafers cut from a cylindrical ingot

summary.kid: The crystal grows like a cylinder, so slicing it makes round wafers.
summary.nerd: Modern wafers are circular because they are sliced from cylindrical single-crystal ingots.

deeper.kid: Later, the chip patterns are square, but they start on a round slice.
deeper.nerd: Rectangular dies are patterned across the circular wafer, leaving partial edge dies that usually cannot be sold.

imageAlt.kid: A wire saw slicing a crystal
imageAlt.nerd: Diamond wire saw cutting silicon wafers

summary.kid: Tiny diamond bits help saw the crystal into thin wafers.
summary.nerd: Diamond wire saws cut hard silicon ingots into wafers, but every cut wastes some material as kerf.

deeper.kid: Careful slicing means more useful wafers from the same crystal.
deeper.nerd: Wafering trades throughput, thickness, breakage, and material loss; better slicing raises usable wafer output.

body.kid: You grew a silicon crystal and sliced it into wafers. Next, you will print tiny circuits on them.
body.nerd: Chapter 3 produced wafer substrates with a carried quality score. Chapter 4 will turn wafer quality into fabrication yield.

subtitle.kid: Print tiny circuits on wafers and keep the good dies.
subtitle.nerd: Pattern, etch, and dope wafers while managing process yield across smaller nodes.

nextChapter.nerd: Continue to Chapter 5: Packaging and Binning

coatHint.kid: Drag across the wafer to spread the blue coat evenly.
coatHint.nerd: Drag over the wafer to maximize photoresist coverage and coating evenness.

exposeHint.kid: Line up the glowing mask, then flash it.
exposeHint.nerd: Align the mask near the target crosshair before UV exposure.

etchHint.kid: Hold in the bath. Release near the target time.
etchHint.nerd: Hold etch dwell close to the process target to avoid under- or over-etch.

dopeHint.kid: Tap the color zones in the requested order.
dopeHint.nerd: Select implant zones that match the requested dopant sequence.

reviewHint.kid: Green dies passed. Red dies get tossed.
reviewHint.nerd: The die map marks saleable dies versus defects from process variation.

needAction.kid: Finish this station before moving on.
needAction.nerd: Current station score is not locked yet.

dustPenalty.nerd: Particle contamination applied a yield penalty to this wafer.

calibrationPenalty.nerd: Calibration drift applied a station score penalty.

text.kid: The wafers are ready. Nova needs working dies, not a perfect-looking trophy.
text.nerd: Fabrication turns blank wafers into patterned dies through coating, lithography, etching, and doping; Nova needs usable yield, not just nominal precision.

text.kid: Then keep the wafer clean and line up each step. Yield is how many chances survive.
text.nerd: Yield depends on process control: particle limits, alignment, dwell timing, and implant accuracy.

text.kid: I want the strongest chips for the clinic, but pushing smaller labels makes each mistake hurt more.
text.nerd: Node names are generation labels, not exact transistor measurements; smaller labels still tighten process control in this game.

imageAlt.kid: A cleanroom suit beside a wafer
imageAlt.nerd: Cleanroom garment used to control particles

summary.kid: The suit keeps skin flakes, hair, and dust away from the wafer.
summary.nerd: Cleanroom garments reduce particles from people, one of the largest contamination sources in wafer fabs.

deeper.kid: The suit protects the chip more than the worker.
deeper.nerd: Fabrication tools and rooms control airflow, filtration, garments, and protocols because tiny particles can ruin patterned features.

imageAlt.kid: A dust speck looming over tiny circuits
imageAlt.nerd: Particle shown larger than nanoscale features

summary.kid: A dust speck is enormous compared with tiny chip parts.
summary.nerd: Modern chip features are so small that ordinary particles can cover or distort many device structures.

deeper.kid: That is why the cleanroom matters so much.
deeper.nerd: Yield engineering tracks defects per area because larger wafers and denser patterns create many opportunities for a tiny flaw to kill a die.

imageAlt.kid: A huge machine shining light through a mask
imageAlt.nerd: EUV scanner representing advanced lithography

summary.kid: The most advanced fabs use giant machines to print the smallest patterns.
summary.nerd: Advanced nodes use extreme ultraviolet lithography for their most intricate layers; ASML describes EUV as unique to its systems.

deeper.kid: Smaller patterns can make faster chips, but the machines are harder to build.
deeper.nerd: EUV systems combine precision optics, vacuum, light generation, stages, masks, and process control, which is why leading-edge fabrication is so capital intensive.

body.kid: You printed circuits onto wafers and kept the good dies. Next, you will package and test chips.
body.nerd: Chapter 4 converted wafer quality and process scores into die yield. Chapter 5 packages and bins those chips.

subtitle.kid: Cut dies apart, test them, then meet the chip team.
subtitle.nerd: Dice fabricated wafers, bin dies by test results, and assemble the chip lineup for the data center.

diceHint.kid: Cut the wafer into tiny chip pieces called dies.
diceHint.nerd: Dice the processed wafer into individual dies before packaging and electrical test.

sortHint.kid: Watch the test meter, then send each die to the right bin.
sortHint.nerd: Use the electrical test score to route each die into top, functional, or salvage bins.

correctSort.kid: Good sort. That die landed in the right bin.
correctSort.nerd: Correct bin assignment preserved the die's tested value.

wrongSort.kid: Close, but that die got downgraded one bin.
wrongSort.nerd: Incorrect binning downgraded the die to the next lower commercial bin.

rosterHint.kid: Spend binned dies to build up to four chip friends.
rosterHint.nerd: Allocate tested dies into a limited chip lineup that will matter in the data center.

maxChoices.nerd: The Chapter 5 roster choice limit has been reached.

cantAfford.kid: Not enough binned dies for that chip.
cantAfford.nerd: Current bin inventory cannot pay this chip's package cost.

novaLocked.kid: Nova needs a perfect leading-edge die and unlocks later.
novaLocked.nerd: Nova is reserved for the finale and requires a top-bin leading-edge die.

probePenalty.kid: Noisy testing made the next few scores rougher.
probePenalty.nerd: Probe drift reduced test confidence and can downgrade binning outcomes.

substratePenalty.kid: Cheaper package parts made perfect builds harder.
substratePenalty.nerd: Lower-grade package stock constrained high-bin chip assembly.

text.kid: The wafer has lots of tiny chips on it. Which ones can we trust for Nova?
text.nerd: The wafer holds many fabricated dies. Which ones are reliable enough for the Nova recovery?

text.kid: Not yet. We cut, package, and test them. Cheap parts can work, but reliability decides where they belong.
text.nerd: Next comes dicing, packaging, electrical test, and binning by performance and power behavior.

text.kid: So I can save budget with weaker chips, but I risk starving the final rack.
text.nerd: So one wafer can produce dies for different roles, and the inventory choice becomes a reliability constraint.

imageAlt.kid: A tiny die inside a protective chip package
imageAlt.nerd: Semiconductor die connected inside a package

summary.kid: A bare die is tiny and fragile. The package protects it and gives it pins to talk to the board.
summary.nerd: Packaging protects the die, carries heat away, and provides electrical connections to the larger system.

deeper.kid: The black square you see in a gadget is usually the package, not the bare die.
deeper.nerd: Modern packages can include substrates, interposers, solder balls, heat spreaders, and multiple dies depending on product design.

imageAlt.kid: Three bins labeled perfect, good, and salvage
imageAlt.nerd: Chip dies sorted by electrical test score

summary.kid: Some chips are super fast. Some are slower but still useful, so they sell for different jobs.
summary.nerd: Binning classifies dies by tested speed, power, and functional blocks so more of the wafer can become sellable products.

deeper.kid: That is why two chips from the same wafer can have different prices.
deeper.nerd: Product segmentation often uses test results to decide which frequency, voltage, or enabled-feature tier a die can support.

imageAlt.kid: Several chip characters standing together
imageAlt.nerd: CPU, GPU, memory, storage, networking, and power chips as a lineup

summary.kid: A computer is not one magic chip. It is a team of chips with different jobs.
summary.nerd: Systems combine compute, memory, storage, networking, and power-management silicon rather than relying on a single chip type.

deeper.kid: The next chapter shows why the team matters inside a data center.
deeper.nerd: Data-center performance depends on how specialized chips, power, cooling, storage, and networking work together.

body.kid: You tested your dies and picked a chip team. Now those chips need racks, power, cooling, and a network.
body.nerd: Chapter 5 converted fabricated dies into a selected chip lineup. Chapter 6 installs that lineup into a data center.

subtitle.nerd: Install packaged chips into powered, cooled, networked racks.

buildHint.kid: Build racks, power, cooling, network, and battery before taking big jobs.
buildHint.nerd: Balance rack capacity against power capacity, cooling headroom, network links, and backup energy.

selectRack.kid: Pick a rack, then install a chip.
selectRack.nerd: Select a rack with open slots before installing available packaged chips.

contractReady.nerd: Current installed chips and infrastructure satisfy this contract.

contractBlocked.kid: This job needs more chips or infrastructure.
contractBlocked.nerd: Requirements are not met. Check chips, compute, power, cooling, and network links.

heatWarning.nerd: Thermal load is approaching the throttle threshold.

powerWarning.nerd: Power load exceeds capacity; effective compute is throttled.

novaLocked.kid: Nova needs one perfect leading-edge die.
novaLocked.nerd: The accelerator recap requires one top-bin leading-edge die from Chapter 5.

victoryReady.nerd: The final workload is served; the supply chain has become useful compute.

text.kid: We made the chips. The clinic is still dark. What is missing?
text.nerd: We have packaged chips, but Nova is still offline. What blocks delivered compute?

text.kid: A chip is powerful, but a data center is a team: racks, power, cooling, and network.
text.nerd: Compute only becomes a service when chips are integrated with power delivery, thermal control, networking, and redundancy.

text.kid: I want every watt on compute. You are about to tell me cooling matters just as much.
text.nerd: I want every watt on compute. You are about to tell me the final constraint is system integration, not transistor performance alone.

text.kid: Exactly. Bring Nova online without cooking it, then serve the jobs that light the city.
text.nerd: Exactly. Meet workload requirements while staying inside power and thermal envelopes.

title.kid: A Data Center Is a Team

imageAlt.kid: A rack connected to power, cooling, and network lines
imageAlt.nerd: A compute rack integrated with data-center support systems

summary.kid: Racks hold many computers. Power feeds them. Cooling carries heat away. Networks let them work together.
summary.nerd: Modern data centers combine compute racks, power distribution, thermal systems, storage, networking, backup power, and monitoring.

deeper.kid: The chips are essential, but the building turns them into useful services.
deeper.nerd: The chips are essential, but the facility turns chips into reliable compute by keeping them powered, cooled, connected, and resilient.

imageAlt.kid: Blue cooling fans beside warm racks
imageAlt.nerd: Cooling infrastructure removing heat from dense compute racks

summary.kid: Busy chips get hot. If they get too hot, they slow down to protect themselves.
summary.nerd: High utilization converts electrical energy into heat. Servers throttle or shut down when cooling cannot maintain safe operating temperatures.

deeper.kid: Cooling is why data centers have fans, chillers, water loops, or other ways to move heat away.
deeper.nerd: Thermal design affects uptime, performance, power use, and where facilities can be built economically.

imageAlt.kid: Green network lines linking several racks
imageAlt.nerd: Network spine connecting compute racks

summary.kid: One rack is useful. Connected racks can act like one bigger computer.
summary.nerd: Low-latency networking lets workloads span machines, storage, and accelerators.

deeper.kid: That is why The Messenger matters. Racks need to talk fast.
deeper.nerd: Network bottlenecks can limit useful compute even when chips are available, especially for distributed AI and storage-heavy services.

body.kid: You turned rocks into chips, chips into racks, and racks into a city service. Sam's tablet turns on.
body.nerd: The run connected mineral extraction, refining, crystal growth, fabrication, packaging, and data-center integration into delivered compute.

tablet.nerd: Powered by your completed semiconductor supply chain

caption.nerd: Mineral supply constrains the semiconductor stack before any wafer exists.
Purity, energy, and waste determine usable inputs.
Wafer quality sets up the fab yield curve.
Process control determines how many good dies survive.

caption.kid: The city finally used the chips.
caption.nerd: Power, cooling, networking, and software turn chips into delivered services.

subtitle.kid: Bring Nova back for the clinic, then trace every rescue choice through the chip supply chain.
subtitle.nerd: Keep a public-interest Nova workload online under power, cooling, yield, and supply-chain constraints.

crisisDescription.nerd: Cold-start the public-interest Nova rescue under power and cooling pressure

accuracyNote.nerd: Educational abstractions are gameplay approximations, with source notes in the Codex.

creditsNote.nerd: Credits: Muhammad Umar Zafar; AI-generated, human-curated art and sound direction.

benchmark.kid: In real mines, copper ore is less than 1% copper. Almost everything you dig up is plain rock.
benchmark.nerd: Typical copper ore grades run below 1% Cu — and a single smartphone draws on roughly 30 mined elements.

handoff.kid: Your minerals ride the rail to the refinery.
handoff.nerd: Concentrate ships to the refinery for smelting and purification.

benchmark.kid: Nine nines is a teaching shortcut for 99.9999999% pure. Chipmaking needs impurities controlled on purpose, not random dirt.
benchmark.nerd: 9N is used here as a purity shorthand: 99.9999999% pure, or roughly one impurity part per billion before intentional doping.

handoff.kid: Your pure silicon heads to the crystal plant.
handoff.nerd: Polysilicon charges ship to the crystal-growth facility.

benchmark.kid: Real crystal pullers grow one giant single crystal, then wire saws slice it into wafers less than 1 mm thick.
benchmark.nerd: Industrial Czochralski pullers grow large single-crystal silicon ingots under controlled heat and rotation; 300 mm wafers are often specified around 775 micrometers thick.

handoff.kid: Your wafers roll into the fab.
handoff.nerd: Wafers enter the fab's front-end process line.

benchmark.kid: A real chip factory repeats careful steps for many weeks: print, etch, clean, check, and repeat until the wafer is ready.
benchmark.nerd: Advanced wafer fabrication can take many weeks and repeat lithography, deposition, etch, clean, implant, inspection, and metrology operations hundreds to thousands of times.

handoff.kid: Your good chips go to packaging.
handoff.nerd: Known-good dies move to assembly, packaging, and test.

benchmark.kid: Inside one package, chips can be stacked like pancakes, joined by bumps thinner than a hair.
benchmark.nerd: Advanced packages stack chiplets on interposers with micro-bump pitches under 50 µm.

handoff.kid: Your chip lineup ships to the data center.
handoff.nerd: Finished parts ship to system integrators and data centers.

benchmark.kid: The biggest data centers use as much electricity as a whole city of homes.
benchmark.nerd: AI-focused data centers can use electricity on the scale of many thousands of homes, so chip efficiency, siting, and cooling matter.

handoff.kid: From rock to rack: you built the whole chain that lights the modern world.
handoff.nerd: From extraction to compute: the chain you just ran underpins effectively all modern infrastructure.
